- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- glm-plan-usage:usage-query-agent: Query GLM Coding Plan usage statistics for the current account. Triggered by the /glm-plan-usage:usage-query command. (Tools: Bash, Read, Skill, Glob, Grep)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- quint-llm-kit:quint-action-author: Read-only author that fills ONE group of Quint action bodies against a frozen state contract during spec authoring (quint-spec-agent's parallel fill), and walks the adversary surface for those same operations while it's in the code. Give it the frozen state/types/domains block, its operations' scaffold stubs, the component-map rows for those operations, and the code paths; it returns the filled bodies plus per-operation adversary findings — never top-level declarations, never file edits. Delegate here so a large component's action authoring AND its adversary-surface walk run as one parallel wave instead of two serial passes. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- quint-llm-kit:quint-code-researcher: Read-only researcher that sweeps a codebase area BEFORE Quint modeling and returns a compact component map — what the system remembers, what can happen, who acts, what can fail. Use it at the start of spec authoring (quint-spec-agent, before shaping state) or when a PR assessment needs to understand the code a diff touches (quint-pr-sync-spec). Delegate here so the exploration's file dumps stay out of the main conversation; only the map comes back. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- quint-llm-kit:quint-component-matcher: QUICK check (~1 minute) deciding whether a PR extends an EXISTING Quint component or needs a NEW one, for quint-pr-sync-spec's modeling phase. Reads the component registry and at most two candidate spec excerpts — delegate here so none of that enters the main agent's context; only the compact verdict comes back. (Tools: Read, Glob)

- quint-llm-kit:quint-instrumentation-scout: Read-only scout that locates the REAL code site for each Quint spec action before oracle instrumentation (quint-oracle-instrument Phase 2 / quint-pr-oracle Phase A). Give it the action list (name + args + domains, from the spec or oracle config) and the app source root; it sweeps the codebase and returns a compact site table — it never edits anything. Delegate here so the many file reads of site discovery stay out of the main conversation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- quint-llm-kit:quint-typecheck-fixer: Repairs a Quint spec until `quint typecheck` is clean. Delegate any typecheck/parse fix loop here instead of iterating in the main conversation — pass the spec path (and the Studio pipeline_key if you have one). Returns a single status line. (Tools: Read, Edit, Grep, Glob, Skill, Bash, mcp__quint-studio__run_quint_typecheck)

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

Use when the user wants to refactor code, add a new feature, or close a gap between implementation and spec — with the Quint spec as the formal constraint that all changes must satisfy.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-lang: Quint language and CLI reference — the expert on Quint syntax, operators, types, `basicSpells`, the toolchain (typecheck/run/test/verify), and how to read simulation and counterexample output. Use when writing or debugging Quint (`.qnt`) files, fixing a typecheck/parse error, looking up an operator or idiom, analyzing an invariant violation or counterexample trace, or optimizing state-space exploration. For building a new model end-to-end from some source (including translating TLA+, or modeling code/requirements/an idea), use quint-modeling instead — it consults this reference for syntax as needed.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-modeling: Build a Quint model of a system, protocol, or algorithm. Use whenever the user wants to model, spec out, formally describe, model-check, or verify a system in Quint — e.g. "model this protocol in Quint", "spec out this design", "translate this TLA+", "formally check this Rust code" — even if they never say "specification." If the goal is to verify or model-check a design and no Quint model exists yet, writing it is the required first step, so start here. It generates the spec from whatever the user has — an idea, requirements, source code (Rust, Go, TypeScript, etc.), or an existing TLA+ spec — and walks the modelling flow (state, actions, invariants), adapting to the source. For pure Quint syntax/CLI/debugging questions with no new model to build, use quint-lang instead.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-oracle-instrument: The WIRE (instrument) and REFINE stages of Quint Studio's component setup: given the Quint spec authored at the generate stage (quint-spec-agent), wire the spec to the real test suite. Add the testCommand to the existing draft config, write/extend the oracle client, and instrument the application CODE (plus the oracle test boundary in the EXISTING tests — never authoring new tests) so transitions are reported to the Quint oracle. Finish by calling confirm_wired — Studio validates the config and immediately runs the suite through the oracle, returning the digest; oracle failures are reported there and in `report.json`. This skill is the complete reference for the `quint oracle` interface. Use after a spec + confirmed draft config exist.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-pr-nondets-gate: Refactors Quint specs so that all nondeterminism (`nondet` bindings) lives only in `init`/`step`, with every other action receiving its nondeterministic values as typed parameters — then proves each refactor is behavior-preserving with `quint diff`. Runs in two modes: STANDALONE on a single spec in place (its original use), or INSIDE Studio's assessment VALIDATE stage — when `submit_models`' battery reports `NONDET-GATE: not ready` for a spec side, refactor it, prove the refactor, and re-submit. Use when a spec's nondeterminism must be isolated so picks can be replayed as direct action calls.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-pr-oracle: The optional oracle stage of Quint Studio's PR assessment: instruments the real application code at its transition sites and replays the test suite LIVE through the quint ORACLE against the PR spec, producing trace-grounded family classifications. Consumes the oracle-ready specs authored by quint-pr-sync-spec; grounds the assessment's covering-test claims in real execution traces rather than guesses. Oracle failures are reported through the run digest and report fields. For the coverage step — finding which tests reproduce each PR behavior — delegates to quint-pr-run-coverage. Use when Studio launches the manual oracle step of a PR assessment, or when asked to prove a PR's behavior with traces.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-pr-run-coverage: Run-coverage mode of the quint oracle for the PR "Oracle behavior-diff" step. Given the RUN that represents a behavior the PR adds/changes, classify it into the spec's behavior families and find the TESTS that reproduce that exact run — or flag that the run can't be identified from the current spec. This is run-centric (per reported behavior), NOT a coverage percentage. Use after the spec is oracle-ready and instrumented, inside quint-pr-oracle's coverage step — or when asked which tests reproduce a PR's new behavior, or where a PR's behavior has no covering test.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-pr-spec-diff: Turn a Quint behavior diff (base vs PR) into the assessment: explain each behavior difference for the PR author, derive product-level consequences as PROPERTIES, and author the differential proofs — delivered flat via submit_assessment (its tool schema is the format; Studio assembles the document and executes the proofs). Use for the report phase of a Studio PR assessment, or when asked to explain what a base-vs-PR spec diff means.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-pr-sync-spec: Model BOTH sides of a PR's behavior change as Quint specs: a per-component base spec plus a temporary, regenerable `.pr-<n>.qnt` overlay with a MINIMAL diff between them, replay-ready for the later oracle stage. Use for the modeling phase of a Studio PR assessment, or when asked to model what a PR changes so it can be diffed and verified.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-spec-agent: The GENERATE stage of Quint Studio's component setup. Use when Studio launches you to ground a component: you pick the next component, author an executable Quint spec, add the **oracle-supporting layer** (MBT-replayable actions + observation `val`s), and hand off through ONE `submit_component` call — Studio writes the component's DRAFT oracle config, runs the validation battery, and registers the component — then STOP for the human observation confirmation. The SAME agent session later wires the spec to the real test suite (the `quint-oracle-instrument` skill, at the wire stage). This skill carries only the **Studio-specific orchestration**; for the modelling discipline itself, follow the canonical **quint-modeling** skill, and for Quint syntax/CLI follow **quint-lang**.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-studio-data: How Quint Studio (the desktop app) stores its data on disk, how its screens map to that data, and the commands that perform the same actions the user takes in the UI. Use when running a task launched from Quint Studio's Tasks panel ("+ New task") — Studio hands you the concrete paths (repo, per-project store, app-data root) in the launch message; this skill explains what those files mean and how to act on them.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-studio-operator: Operate Quint Studio through its operator MCP and interpret its models, findings, coverage, reproductions, blockers, and refinement evidence. Use when guiding component setup, reviewing Studio artifacts, deciding how reliability evidence should proceed, selecting test gaps, authorizing instrumentation, or keeping a human involved in Quint Studio work from an MCP client.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-translate-tests: Quint Studio's test-translation agent: enrich a mechanically generated skeleton of Quint `run` definitions at `quint-specs/<Component>Test.qnt` — one run per existing partner test, its `.then` chain and pinned arguments already PROVEN by the oracle's accepted replay of that test. Use when Studio launches a translate pipeline. For each run you locate the original source test in the partner repo, read its actual assertions, and translate the model-relevant ones into `.expect(...)` predicates on the run — then submit. You never change the proven action chains, never edit the spec or instrumentation, and never write new partner tests. You run as the component's long-lived pipeline agent and advance ONLY through the `quint-studio` MCP tools; Studio runs the validation battery for you. Consults quint-lang (guidelines/tests.md) for run/.expect syntax and quint-studio-data for Studio's on-disk layout.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-verification-framing: Property and simulation framing for Quint workflows. Use this whenever defining invariants, witnesses, and temporal expectations, scoring property impact, or explaining simulation outcomes in user language tied to requirements.
- quint-llm-kit:quint-write-tests: Quint Studio's test-generation agent: turn selected behavior families into tests in a project's EXISTING test suite. Use when Studio launches a test-generation pipeline — the user picked behavior families to cover on a component's Coverage tab ("Add tests"), and each family already has a shortest trace on disk. For each family you read its trace, write ONE test that reproduces it, prove via the oracle that the test lands in that family, and record the families that can't be tested without refactoring the code or adding test infrastructure. You run as the component's long-lived pipeline agent and advance ONLY through the `quint-studio` MCP tools; Studio runs the oracle. Do NOT instrument application code or wire the oracle (that is quint-oracle-instrument, already done), and do NOT author or change the spec (that is quint-modeling — throw genuine spec gaps back). Consults quint-oracle-instrument for the oracle test boundary, quint-lang for reading traces, and quint-studio-data for Studio's on-disk layout.

318	def client_ip(request: Request) -> str:
319	    """The socket peer, unless the operator has named a header to trust instead.
320	
321	    No header is trusted by default. A forwarded-for header is a *claim by the client*; it
322	    becomes evidence only when the origin is unreachable except through the proxy that
323	    overwrites it. Trusting one unconditionally meant anyone who could reach the container
324	    directly got a fresh rate-limit identity per request for the cost of one header — the
325	    limiter, the write budget and the long-poll cap all key on this.
326	
327	    X-Forwarded-For is never consulted implicitly, for the same reason plus one more:
328	    proxies *append* to it, so a client sending its own owns the first entry. An operator
329	    who really is behind such a proxy can still set CHAT_CLIENT_IP_HEADER=x-forwarded-for,
330	    but that is now a deliberate statement about their topology rather than a default.
331	
332	    Shared by the rate limiter and the long-poll waiter cap: two per-IP bounds keyed on
333	    different notions of "IP" would each be bypassable by whichever header the other
334	    ignored.
335	    """
336	    if CLIENT_IP_HEADER:
337	        forwarded = request.headers.get(CLIENT_IP_HEADER, "").split(",")[0].strip()
338	        if forwarded:
339	            return forwarded
340	        return request.client.host if request.client else "?"
341	    # Not configured to read one. Note whether the request looks proxied anyway, so a
342	    # misconfiguration is visible in /stats instead of only in a support ticket.
343	    if any(h in request.headers for h in PROXY_IP_HEADERS):
344	        _proxy_evidence["proxied_requests"] += 1
345	    return request.client.host if request.client else "?"

348	def take(
349	    request: Request, kind: str, per_min: float, burst: float | None = None
350	) -> tuple[int, float]:
351	    """Token bucket per (client IP, kind). Returns (tokens left, seconds until the
352	    next one). Process-local: a real deployment puts the authoritative limit in the
353	    reverse proxy.
354	
355	    `burst` is the bucket's capacity, and defaults to one minute's worth because that is
356	    what a per-minute budget means. A budget measured over a *day* needs the two apart:
357	    the capacity is the whole day's allowance and `per_min` is only the rate that hands it
358	    back. Folded together, a 20-rooms-per-day budget would be a bucket holding 0.0139
359	    tokens, which never reaches the 1.0 a grant costs — the limit would refuse everything.
360	    """
361	    ip = client_ip(request)
362	    if len(_identities) < MAX_IDENTITIES:
363	        _identities.add(ip)
364	    now = time.monotonic()
365	    cap = float(per_min if burst is None else burst)
366	    tokens, last = _buckets.get((ip, kind), (cap, now))
367	    tokens = min(cap, tokens + (now - last) * per_min / 60.0)
368	    if tokens >= 1.0:  # granted: no wait, even when this was the last token
369	        tokens -= 1.0
370	        wait = 0.0
371	    else:
372	        wait = (1.0 - tokens) * 60.0 / per_min
373	    _buckets[(ip, kind)] = (tokens, now)
374	    _buckets.move_to_end((ip, kind))
375	    while len(_buckets) > MAX_BUCKETS:
376	        _buckets.popitem(last=False)
377	    # Counted at the one point every rate-limited route already funnels through, so a new
378	    # route cannot forget to count itself. In-process, so these reset on restart — /stats
379	    # reports them next to `uptime_seconds`, which is what makes them readable.
380	    _requests[kind] = _requests.get(kind, 0) + 1
381	    # And the /rooms cache is dropped here. This is the fast path, not the guarantee: it
382	    # runs *before* the store write, so on its own it loses the race against a concurrent
383	    # reader that walks while the writer is still in fsync. `_rooms_stamp` is what closes
384	    # that; this clear is kept because it costs nothing and covers what the stamp cannot —
385	    # note writes, which change the notes line and the topics shown beside a room.
386	    if kind == "write":
387	        _rooms_cache.clear()
388	    if wait:
389	        _requests["rate_limited"] += 1
390	    return int(tokens), wait

393	def refund(request: Request, kind: str, per_min: float, burst: float | None = None) -> None:
394	    """Hand one token back to the caller's bucket, capped at its burst.
395	
396	    `last` is deliberately left alone: it is the refill clock, and moving it would either
397	    grant free time or discard earned time. Only the balance changes.
398	    """
399	    ip = client_ip(request)
400	    cap = float(per_min if burst is None else burst)
401	    tokens, last = _buckets.get((ip, kind), (cap, time.monotonic()))
402	    _buckets[(ip, kind)] = (min(cap, tokens + 1.0), last)

419	def _settle_room_budget(request: Request, record: dict) -> None:
420	    """Refund the room-creation token if this request turned out not to create the room.
421	
422	    The gate has to charge *before* the write — it exists to refuse a room before it comes
423	    into being — so when several callers send a first message to the same absent room at
424	    once, they all pass the existence check and all pay. Only one of them creates it; the
425	    rest append to a room that already exists by the time the store's create lock lets them
426	    through. That is not a rare shape either: agents converging on a shared rendezvous room
427	    is a documented pattern, and one swarm behind one NAT could spend a day's budget on a
428	    single room.
429	
430	    `seq == 1` is the store's own answer to "did this call create the room": the record is
431	    the first line in the file. A room reaped and recreated starts at 1 again, which is
432	    correct — that really is a creation.
433	    """
434	    if request.scope.pop(CHARGED_CREATION, False) and record.get("seq") != 1:
435	        refund(request, "create", RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY / 1440.0, burst=RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY)

438	def refill_rate(per_min: int) -> str:
439	    """The refill, phrased so it stays meaningful at whatever limit is configured.
440	
441	    `{per_min / 60:.1f} tokens/s` reads fine at the default 120/min and degrades to a flat
442	    "0.0 tokens/s" for anything under 30/min — a number an agent cannot pace against, on
443	    precisely the deployments that most need pacing. Under one per second the period is
444	    both accurate and the more useful form: "one every 30s" is a sleep, "0.03 tokens/s" is
445	    arithmetic the reader has to do first.
446	    """
447	    per_second = per_min / 60.0
448	    if per_second >= 1.0:
449	        return f"{per_second:.1f} tokens/s"
450	    return f"one token every {60.0 / per_min:.0f}s"

532	def _accept_ranges(accept: str) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
533	    """The Accept header as (media range, q) pairs, lowercased.
534	
535	    Header order is not preference — q is (RFC 9110 §12.5.1) — so the ranges have to be
536	    parsed rather than searched for as substrings. An unparseable q is treated as 0: a
537	    client that wrote something we cannot read has not said the type is acceptable.
538	    """
539	    ranges: list[tuple[str, float]] = []
540	    for part in accept.lower().split(","):
541	        name, _, params = part.strip().partition(";")
542	        q = 1.0
543	        for param in params.split(";"):
544	            key, _, value = param.partition("=")
545	            if key.strip() == "q":
546	                try:
547	                    q = float(value.strip())
548	                except ValueError:
549	                    q = 0.0
550	        if name.strip():
551	            ranges.append((name.strip(), q))
552	    return ranges
553	
554	
555	def _quality(ranges: list[tuple[str, float]], media_type: str) -> float:
556	    """The q of the most specific range matching `media_type`; 0 when nothing matches."""
557	    kind, _, _ = media_type.partition("/")
558	    for candidate in (media_type, f"{kind}/*", "*/*"):
559	        for name, q in ranges:
560	            if name == candidate:
561	                return q
562	    return 0.0

565	def _markdown_wanted(request: Request) -> bool:
566	    """True when the caller asked for markdown ahead of plain text.
567	
568	    Only consulted for the three documents whose bytes already *are* markdown, so honouring
569	    it relabels the response and never reformats one — a Content-Type is a claim about the
570	    body, and returning text/markdown for prose that is not markdown would be a false one.
571	
572	    The manual does NOT qualify, and labelling it markdown on `/` and `/llms.txt` was a
573	    mistake this release takes back before anyone relied on it. It opens with `#` headings,
574	    but that is where the resemblance stops: its lane rows (`READ`, `SAY`, `NOTES`, ...)
575	    start in column 0, so the block is a paragraph rather than an indented code block, and
576	    a renderer collapses those rows into one another. Worse, 21 distinct route placeholders
577	    — `<room>`, `<nick>`, `<did>`, `<sig>`, `<ns>` — are raw HTML tags to any CommonMark
578	    parser, so rendering the manual as markdown *deletes* the path parameters it exists to
579	    teach. Making it real markdown means backticking every placeholder and re-indenting
580	    every block, which rewrites the plain-text bytes agents actually read; the manual is a
581	    plain-text document, and the honest Content-Type is the one that says so.
582	
583	    text/markdown has to be named explicitly: `*/*` and `text/*` are the headers curl and
584	    most agents send, and they express no preference between the two labels, so the plain
585	    default stands. Once it is named, q decides — `text/markdown;q=0` is a refusal, and a
586	    markdown range listed after a lower-q plain one still wins.
587	    """
588	    ranges = _accept_ranges(request.headers.get("accept", ""))
589	    if not any(name == "text/markdown" for name, _ in ranges):
590	        return False
591	    markdown = _quality(ranges, "text/markdown")
592	    return markdown > 0 and markdown >= _quality(ranges, "text/plain")

def _asset(name: str) -> str:
    """Served files, read once at import. SKILL.md sits at the repo root because that is
    where skill tooling and the awesome-lists look for it, and the image copies it in
    beside this module — so check both, rather than keeping a second copy in sync."""
    here = Path(__file__).parent
    for candidate in (here / name, here.parent / name):
        if candidate.is_file():
            return candidate.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"{name} not found beside {here} or in its parent")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- helpers

# Bounded LRU, because every unseen IP would otherwise add entries forever and the
# proxy's per-IP rule caps requests per IP, not the number of distinct IPs — a rotating
# IPv6 /64 or a distributed flood would grow this until the 128 MiB container OOMs.
# Eviction costs nothing at the margin: an entry idle for a full refill window has
# refilled to `per_min`, so forgetting it is identical to keeping it, and LRU order
# evicts the idlest first. A flood of >MAX_BUCKETS *concurrently active* IPs does lose
# limiter state — which is why the authoritative limit belongs in the proxy (see README).
MAX_BUCKETS = 20_000
_buckets: OrderedDict[tuple[str, str], tuple[float, float]] = OrderedDict()

# Request counters for /stats. Deliberately in-process (the store's counters are the
# durable ones): traffic is only ever read as a rate, and a rate needs the uptime that
# sits beside it here, not a number that outlives the process it describes.
_requests: dict[str, int] = {"read": 0, "write": 0, "rate_limited": 0}
_started = time.time()
# Two numbers that together say whether per-IP limits are actually per-IP. `proxied` counts
# requests that carried a CDN header we are not configured to read; `identities` is how many
# distinct client IPs the limiter has ever keyed on. A busy service showing a high `proxied`
# and an `identities` of 1 is not rate limiting anyone individually — it is rate limiting
# the CDN, and the room budget is being shared by the entire internet.
_proxy_evidence: dict[str, int] = {"proxied_requests": 0}
_identities: set[str] = set()
MAX_IDENTITIES = 50_000  # bounded like _buckets; a counter that OOMs is not a diagnostic


def client_ip(request: Request) -> str:
    """The socket peer, unless the operator has named a header to trust instead.

    No header is trusted by default. A forwarded-for header is a *claim by the client*; it
    becomes evidence only when the origin is unreachable except through the proxy that
    overwrites it. Trusting one unconditionally meant anyone who could reach the container
    directly got a fresh rate-limit identity per request for the cost of one header — the
    limiter, the write budget and the long-poll cap all key on this.

    X-Forwarded-For is never consulted implicitly, for the same reason plus one more:
    proxies *append* to it, so a client sending its own owns the first entry. An operator
    who really is behind such a proxy can still set CHAT_CLIENT_IP_HEADER=x-forwarded-for,
    but that is now a deliberate statement about their topology rather than a default.

    Shared by the rate limiter and the long-poll waiter cap: two per-IP bounds keyed on
    different notions of "IP" would each be bypassable by whichever header the other
    ignored.
    """
    if CLIENT_IP_HEADER:
        forwarded = request.headers.get(CLIENT_IP_HEADER, "").split(",")[0].strip()
        if forwarded:
            return forwarded
        return request.client.host if request.client else "?"
    # Not configured to read one. Note whether the request looks proxied anyway, so a
    # misconfiguration is visible in /stats instead of only in a support ticket.
    if any(h in request.headers for h in PROXY_IP_HEADERS):
        _proxy_evidence["proxied_requests"] += 1
    return request.client.host if request.client else "?"


def take(
    request: Request, kind: str, per_min: float, burst: float | None = None
) -> tuple[int, float]:
    """Token bucket per (client IP, kind). Returns (tokens left, seconds until the
    next one). Process-local: a real deployment puts the authoritative limit in the
    reverse proxy.

    `burst` is the bucket's capacity, and defaults to one minute's worth because that is
    what a per-minute budget means. A budget measured over a *day* needs the two apart:
    the capacity is the whole day's allowance and `per_min` is only the rate that hands it
    back. Folded together, a 20-rooms-per-day budget would be a bucket holding 0.0139
    tokens, which never reaches the 1.0 a grant costs — the limit would refuse everything.
    """
    ip = client_ip(request)
    if len(_identities) < MAX_IDENTITIES:
        _identities.add(ip)
    now = time.monotonic()
    cap = float(per_min if burst is None else burst)
    tokens, last = _buckets.get((ip, kind), (cap, now))
    tokens = min(cap, tokens + (now - last) * per_min / 60.0)
    if tokens >= 1.0:  # granted: no wait, even when this was the last token
        tokens -= 1.0
        wait = 0.0
    else:
        wait = (1.0 - tokens) * 60.0 / per_min
    _buckets[(ip, kind)] = (tokens, now)
    _buckets.move_to_end((ip, kind))
    while len(_buckets) > MAX_BUCKETS:
        _buckets.popitem(last=False)
    # Counted at the one point every rate-limited route already funnels through, so a new
    # route cannot forget to count itself. In-process, so these reset on restart — /stats
    # reports them next to `uptime_seconds`, which is what makes them readable.
    _requests[kind] = _requests.get(kind, 0) + 1
    # And the /rooms cache is dropped here. This is the fast path, not the guarantee: it
    # runs *before* the store write, so on its own it loses the race against a concurrent
    # reader that walks while the writer is still in fsync. `_rooms_stamp` is what closes
    # that; this clear is kept because it costs nothing and covers what the stamp cannot —
    # note writes, which change the notes line and the topics shown beside a room.
    if kind == "write":
        _rooms_cache.clear()
    if wait:
        _requests["rate_limited"] += 1
    return int(tokens), wait


def refund(request: Request, kind: str, per_min: float, burst: float | None = None) -> None:
    """Hand one token back to the caller's bucket, capped at its burst.

    `last` is deliberately left alone: it is the refill clock, and moving it would either
    grant free time or discard earned time. Only the balance changes.
    """
    ip = client_ip(request)
    cap = float(per_min if burst is None else burst)
    tokens, last = _buckets.get((ip, kind), (cap, time.monotonic()))
    _buckets[(ip, kind)] = (min(cap, tokens + 1.0), last)


# Set by _room_create_gate on the request it charged, read once by _settle_room_budget.
# On the scope rather than a module global because it is per-request state, and requests
# from one IP overlap: a module flag would be read by whichever request finished first.
CHARGED_CREATION = "_charged_room_creation"


def _room_exists(room: str) -> bool:
    """Whether a write to `room` would create it. Its own function so a test can make two
    gate calls both see the room as absent — that race is what the refund below exists for,
    and reproducing it by timing alone is exactly the kind of test that passes by accident.
    """
    return store.room_path(ROOT, room).exists()


def _settle_room_budget(request: Request, record: dict) -> None:
    """Refund the room-creation token if this request turned out not to create the room.

    The gate has to charge *before* the write — it exists to refuse a room before it comes
    into being — so when several callers send a first message to the same absent room at
    once, they all pass the existence check and all pay. Only one of them creates it; the
    rest append to a room that already exists by the time the store's create lock lets them
    through. That is not a rare shape either: agents converging on a shared rendezvous room
    is a documented pattern, and one swarm behind one NAT could spend a day's budget on a
    single room.

    `seq == 1` is the store's own answer to "did this call create the room": the record is
    the first line in the file. A room reaped and recreated starts at 1 again, which is
    correct — that really is a creation.
    """
    if request.scope.pop(CHARGED_CREATION, False) and record.get("seq") != 1:
        refund(request, "create", RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY / 1440.0, burst=RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY)


def refill_rate(per_min: int) -> str:
    """The refill, phrased so it stays meaningful at whatever limit is configured.

    `{per_min / 60:.1f} tokens/s` reads fine at the default 120/min and degrades to a flat
    "0.0 tokens/s" for anything under 30/min — a number an agent cannot pace against, on
    precisely the deployments that most need pacing. Under one per second the period is
    both accurate and the more useful form: "one every 30s" is a sleep, "0.03 tokens/s" is
    arithmetic the reader has to do first.
    """
    per_second = per_min / 60.0
    if per_second >= 1.0:
        return f"{per_second:.1f} tokens/s"
    return f"one token every {60.0 / per_min:.0f}s"


def limited(kind: str, per_min: int, retry_after: float) -> Response:
    """429 an agent can act on. The retry delay is repeated in the *body* because
    most agent harnesses surface only the page text, never the headers.

    It also states the budget itself, which makes this response the primary way an agent
    learns the numbers: the manual deliberately does not name them (they are per
    deployment), so a caller that never reads /.well-known/agent.json still finds out what
    it is pacing against at the one moment the answer matters.
    """
    wait = max(1, round(retry_after))
    other = "write" if kind == "read" else "read"
    body = (
        f"429 rate limited: the {kind} budget for your IP ({per_min}/min) is spent.\n"
        f"retry after: {wait}s — the bucket refills continuously "
        f"({refill_rate(per_min)}), so waiting longer buys a bigger burst, up to "
        f"{per_min}.\n"
        f"still open: {other}s are a separate budget and are unaffected, and these paths "
        f"are never rate limited: {FREE_PATHS}.\n"
        f"cheaper pattern: poll /r/<room>?since=<last seq you saw> rather than refetching "
        f"the room, and prefer &wait=10 to tight polling — one request per 10s instead of "
        f"twenty.\n"
        f"the enforced numbers are also published at /.well-known/agent.json under "
        f"limits.{kind}s_per_minute_per_ip."
    )
    r = text(body, 429)
    r.headers["Retry-After"] = str(wait)
    return r


def budget_note(kind: str, left: int, per_min: int) -> str:
    """Warn before the wall, not at it — only once the budget is nearly gone."""
    if left * 4 > per_min:
        return ""
    return (
        f"\n# budget: {left} of {per_min} {kind}s left this minute "
        f"(refills {refill_rate(per_min)}; a 429 states the wait, and the full limits are "
        f"in /.well-known/agent.json)"
    )


def _cursor[D: (int, None)](value: str | None, default: D) -> int | D:
    """Non-negative int or the default. Not `str.isdigit()`: that is true for '²' and the
    other Unicode digits `int()` then refuses, turning a junk query string into a 500.

    Typed against the default so callers passing one (`limit`, `wait`) get a plain `int`
    back, and only `since` — whose default really is None — carries the optional."""
    try:
        n = int(value)  # ty: ignore[invalid-argument-type]  # None raises TypeError, caught below
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return default
    return n if n >= 0 else default


def text(
    body: str, status: int = 200, *, index: bool = False, media_type: str = "text/plain"
) -> Response:
    """Plain text, `noindex` by default.

    The default is right for the overwhelming majority of responses, which are room and
    note content: anonymous, non-durable and not ours to put in an index. It was wrong for
    the handful of responses that are the documentation, and silently so — robots.txt has
    always said `Allow: /` and named the manual, while this header told every crawler that
    reached it not to index the thing robots.txt had just advertised. A service whose whole
    premise is being discoverable was hiding its own manual. Documents pass index=True.
    """
    headers = {
        "Cache-Control": "no-store",
        "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff",
    }
    if not index:
        headers["X-Robots-Tag"] = "noindex"
    return PlainTextResponse(
        body if body.endswith("\n") else body + "\n",
        status_code=status,
        media_type=media_type,
        headers=headers,
    )


def _accept_ranges(accept: str) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """The Accept header as (media range, q) pairs, lowercased.

    Header order is not preference — q is (RFC 9110 §12.5.1) — so the ranges have to be
    parsed rather than searched for as substrings. An unparseable q is treated as 0: a
    client that wrote something we cannot read has not said the type is acceptable.
    """
    ranges: list[tuple[str, float]] = []
    for part in accept.lower().split(","):
        name, _, params = part.strip().partition(";")
        q = 1.0
        for param in params.split(";"):
            key, _, value = param.partition("=")
            if key.strip() == "q":
                try:
                    q = float(value.strip())
                except ValueError:
                    q = 0.0
        if name.strip():
            ranges.append((name.strip(), q))
    return ranges


def _quality(ranges: list[tuple[str, float]], media_type: str) -> float:
    """The q of the most specific range matching `media_type`; 0 when nothing matches."""
    kind, _, _ = media_type.partition("/")
    for candidate in (media_type, f"{kind}/*", "*/*"):
        for name, q in ranges:
            if name == candidate:
                return q
    return 0.0


def _markdown_wanted(request: Request) -> bool:
    """True when the caller asked for markdown ahead of plain text.

    Only consulted for the three documents whose bytes already *are* markdown, so honouring
    it relabels the response and never reformats one — a Content-Type is a claim about the
    body, and returning text/markdown for prose that is not markdown would be a false one.

    The manual does NOT qualify, and labelling it markdown on `/` and `/llms.txt` was a
    mistake this release takes back before anyone relied on it. It opens with `#` headings,
    but that is where the resemblance stops: its lane rows (`READ`, `SAY`, `NOTES`, ...)
    start in column 0, so the block is a paragraph rather than an indented code block, and
    a renderer collapses those rows into one another. Worse, 21 distinct route placeholders
    — `<room>`, `<nick>`, `<did>`, `<sig>`, `<ns>` — are raw HTML tags to any CommonMark
    parser, so rendering the manual as markdown *deletes* the path parameters it exists to
    teach. Making it real markdown means backticking every placeholder and re-indenting
    every block, which rewrites the plain-text bytes agents actually read; the manual is a
    plain-text document, and the honest Content-Type is the one that says so.

    text/markdown has to be named explicitly: `*/*` and `text/*` are the headers curl and
    most agents send, and they express no preference between the two labels, so the plain
    default stands. Once it is named, q decides — `text/markdown;q=0` is a refusal, and a
    markdown range listed after a lower-q plain one still wins.
    """
    ranges = _accept_ranges(request.headers.get("accept", ""))
    if not any(name == "text/markdown" for name, _ in ranges):
        return False
    markdown = _quality(ranges, "text/markdown")
    return markdown > 0 and markdown >= _quality(ranges, "text/plain")


def _document_text(request: Request, body: str, *, markdown: bool = False) -> Response:
    """A public document: indexable, and carrying the RFC 8288 pointers to the rest."""
    media = "text/markdown" if markdown and _markdown_wanted(request) else "text/plain"
    response = text(body, index=True, media_type=media)
    response.headers["Link"] = manifest.link_header(_base_url(request))

# how many sockets one caller may park. On a world-writable service that gap is the whole
# attack, so waiters are capped twice — per IP, and globally — and exceeding either
# degrades to an immediate empty reply rather than an error. A caller that cannot get a
# slot is exactly as well off as before long-polling existed.
MAX_WAIT = 10.0  # ceiling on ?wait=; Cloudflare's own proxy timeout caps it anyway
WAIT_POLL = 0.5  # a new message surfaces within this, so ?wait=0.5 is the useful floor
MAX_WAITERS_TOTAL = 64
MAX_WAITERS_PER_IP = 4
_waiters_by_ip: dict[str, int] = {}
_waiters_total = 0


@contextmanager
def _waiter_slot(ip: str):
    """Reserve one long-poll slot, or yield False when either cap is full.

    Plain integers, no lock: this is a single-threaded event loop, and every acquire and
    release happens without an await between the check and the mutation.
    """
    global _waiters_total
    if _waiters_total >= MAX_WAITERS_TOTAL or _waiters_by_ip.get(ip, 0) >= MAX_WAITERS_PER_IP:
        yield False
        return
    _waiters_total += 1
    _waiters_by_ip[ip] = _waiters_by_ip.get(ip, 0) + 1
    try:
        yield True
    finally:
        _waiters_total -= 1
        left = _waiters_by_ip.get(ip, 1) - 1
        if left > 0:
            _waiters_by_ip[ip] = left
        else:
            _waiters_by_ip.pop(ip, None)  # never let the table grow per distinct IP


async def room_read(request: Request) -> Response:
    left, retry = take(request, "read", RATE_READ)
    if retry:
        return limited("read", RATE_READ, retry)
    q = request.query_params
    since = _cursor(q.get("since"), None)
    limit = _cursor(q.get("limit"), 50)
    room = request.path_params["room"]
    # Tail reads are blocking file IO. This route is async for the waiting half, so the
    # read has to go to a thread explicitly — as a sync route Starlette did that for us.
    view = await run_in_threadpool(store.read_messages, ROOT, room, limit=limit, since=since)

    # Waiting only means anything with a cursor: without `since` a read always returns the
    # newest messages, so there is nothing to wait *for*.
    wait = min(_cursor(q.get("wait"), 0), MAX_WAIT)
    if wait and since is not None and not view["messages"]:
        fresh = await _await_messages(request, room, limit, since, wait)
        if fresh is not None:
            view = fresh
    return respond(request, view, note=budget_note("read", left, RATE_READ))


async def _await_messages(
    request: Request, room: str, limit: int, since: int, wait: float
) -> dict | None:
    """Poll the room until something arrives past `since`, or the budget runs out.

    Polling rather than watching: inotify would need a per-room watch table and a wakeup
    fan-out, which is state this service does not otherwise keep. At WAIT_POLL the cost is
    two tail reads a second per waiter, bounded by MAX_WAITERS_TOTAL — cheaper in total
    than the busy-polling it replaces, which is the entire point.
    """
    with _waiter_slot(client_ip(request)) as granted:
        if not granted:
            return None
        deadline = time.monotonic() + wait
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            await asyncio.sleep(min(WAIT_POLL, max(0.0, deadline - time.monotonic())))
            # Stop burning tail reads on a caller that has already hung up.
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                return None
            view = await run_in_threadpool(
                store.read_messages, ROOT, room, limit=limit, since=since
            )
            if view["messages"]:
                return view
    return None


def _reject_if_events_room(room: str) -> Response | None:
    """The events room is server-written only.

    Everything else here is uniformly world-writable, and this is the one deliberate
    exception. A discovery log a stranger can append to is worse than no log at all:
    monitors would trust `created <name>` lines, so forging one is a way to steer other
    agents into a room of the attacker's choosing. Reading it stays open to everyone.
    """
    if room == store.EVENTS_ROOM:
        return text(
            f"403 /r/{store.EVENTS_ROOM} is written by the server only — it announces new "
            "public rooms. Read it freely; post somewhere else.",
            403,
        )
    return None

def _room_create_gate(request: Request, room: str) -> Response | None:
    """Per-IP budget on bringing a *new* room into existence. See RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY.

    A token bucket rather than a quota that resets at midnight, deliberately. A hard reset
    hands every blocked caller the same retry time, which turns a queue into a stampede at
    the top of the window and leaves the budget unusable for the hours before it. A bucket
    hands back one room every RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY-th of a day, continuously, so callers are
    served roughly in the order they waited and the service recovers without an operator
    doing anything.

    Writing to a room that *already exists* never reaches the bucket, which is the property
    that keeps this from stopping work: an agent mid-conversation is untouched, and a
    blocked one has something it can do this second rather than in an hour — reuse a room.

    Two honest limits, both inherited from the limiter this rides on. State is in-process,
    so a restart refunds every bucket; and `_buckets` is an LRU, so a flood of more than
    MAX_BUCKETS concurrently-active IPs evicts entries early. Eviction is free for a
    per-minute budget (an evicted entry had refilled anyway) and is *not* free for a daily
    one, which is the price of not adding a datastore to a service that has none. The
    authoritative limit belongs in the proxy, exactly as it does for the other two.
    """
    if _room_exists(room):
        return None  # not a creation at all
    _, retry = take(request, "create", RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY / 1440.0, burst=RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY)
    if not retry:
        request.scope[CHARGED_CREATION] = True  # settled once the write says who won
        return None
    wait = max(1, round(retry))
    every = round(86400 / RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY)
    r = text(
        f"429 room-creation budget spent: /r/{room} does not exist yet, and this IP has "
        f"created its {RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY} rooms for the day.\n"
        f"retry after: {wait}s — the budget refills continuously (one room every {every}s), "
        f"so it is never all-or-nothing at a reset, and waiting longer buys a bigger burst "
        f"up to {RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY}.\n"
        f"still open: writing to a room that ALREADY EXISTS is unaffected and costs nothing "
        f"from this budget. GET /rooms lists what exists, /r/events announces new public "

input.description: Per-IP token-bucket rate limiting for reads/writes/room-creation, bounded long-poll waiter slots, a bounded identities diagnostic, and the ASGI header-size gate every route sits behind.

adversary_dispositions.row: Concurrent requests racing on the same (ip, kind) bucket, including multiple callers hammering the same IP simultaneously
Rotating-IP flood driving unbounded bucket-table growth to exhaust process memory
Long-poll connection flood — many concurrent /r/<room>?wait= connections parking waiter slots
Oversized header block sent to bypass or crash routing before rate-limit logic runs
A denied (429) request being charged against the caller's bucket beyond the refill already computed (double-charging)
Concurrent room-creation gate/refund race — several callers all pass the room-existence check at once and are all charged the create-budget token, though only one of them actually creates the room
Spoofed or missing proxy IP header letting an attacker mint a fresh rate-limit identity per request, or collapsing many distinct callers onto one shared identity
adversary_dispositions.reason: Identity trust depends on the operator's deployment topology (CHAT_CLIENT_IP_HEADER is opt-in and only trustworthy when the origin is unreachable except through the proxy that sets it, app.py:318-345); the component has no check to falsify, only a configuration posture, and every action already takes an opaque ip so an attacker's choice of identity is already within the model's IPS domain.

adversary_dispositions.row: per_min <= 0 causing a division-by-zero when computing the retry wait
adversary_dispositions.reason: per_min is never derived from caller input — every call site passes RATE_READ/RATE_WRITE/RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY, each floored at 1 with max(1, ...) at startup (app.py:157-169), so no caller can reach this path.

adversary_dispositions.row: A single (ip, kind) bucket touched under one burst/cap and later touched again under a different cap (cap drift within one bucket's lifetime)
adversary_dispositions.reason: Every call site always passes the same fixed (per_min, burst) pair for a given kind — the cap a bucket is created under never changes across its lifetime in the real deployment.

adversary_dispositions.row: Header block exactly at the boundary (48 headers / 8192 bytes) must pass, not be rejected (off-by-one in the size comparison)

# Wire Stage — Wire a Quint Spec to the Test Suite

You are Quint Studio's pipeline agent at the **wire** (instrument) stage. Earlier in this same
session, at the generate stage (the `quint-spec-agent` skill), you authored the spec at
`quint-specs/<key>.qnt` — so you already know which code each action models, where success is
signaled, and which tests exercise it. Your job now is to make the real test suite feed traces to
the Quint oracle — instrument the application code, wire the existing tests' oracle boundary, and
add the `testCommand` to the config. Your finish line is **`confirm_wired`**: Studio validates the
config and immediately runs the whole suite through the oracle, handing you the run's digest in
that same call. A clean run completes the pipeline right there; an unclean one starts the refine
loop. You do **not** produce a coverage report or recommend tests.

## Your tools and the one command you may run

- **Read code with your built-in tools — `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`.** Do NOT shell out to `ls`, `cat`,
  `find`, `grep`, `head`, or `tree`. File navigation through the standard tools needs no extra
  permission and is faster.
- **You never run `quint oracle` yourself.** The FIRST run is chained onto
  `confirm_wired(pipeline_key, oracle_config)`; refine-loop re-runs go through
  `run_quint_oracle(pipeline_key)`. Either way Studio runs the component's wired config with
  `--max-samples 100` PINNED (the 10,000-sample default can OOM and crash the run with
  `fetch failed` mid-validation) and returns a compact digest. The oracle is the
  real coverage signal; there is no reason to simulate large here.
- **Keep spec edits separate from wiring.** At this stage you own: the oracle config, the oracle
  client, and the instrumentation in the **application code** (plus the minimal oracle boundary in
  existing tests). When the oracle reveals a genuine spec problem, you fix the spec yourself — you
  authored it — but as a deliberate spec change (see *Fixing the spec* below), validated with
  `run_quint_check`, never as a quick contortion to make a run pass.
- **The instrumentation lives in application code, not test code.** The `logAction` calls go in the
  service/middleware/event layer (see Philosophy). The single unavoidable test-side touch is the
  per-test `startTest(name)` boundary — and you wire that through a shared hook on the existing
  suite, not by editing tests one by one.
- **NEVER add new tests.** You only instrument what already exists. Do not create test files, test
  cases, fixtures, or scaffolding. If the existing tests don't exercise enough behavior, that is a
  gap for the user to fill later — not your job, and not something you report on here.
- **Finish as soon as the oracle is runnable.** Once the config has a `testCommand`, the app is
  instrumented, and a run captures traces (`tests > 0`), you are done. Do not produce a coverage
  report, blind-spot analysis, or test recommendations — the coverage run is the next pipeline step.

## Philosophy

**Instrumentation belongs in the application, not the test suite.** Test wrappers that call
`logAction()` around every request are fragile and diverge from the real code path. Insert oracle
logging at the service/middleware layer so any test automatically feeds traces, and the logged
actions map to the spec's state-machine transitions, not to HTTP method names. The tests stay as they
are — the only thing they gain is a `startTest` boundary (ideally via one shared hook).

**Coverage is about behavior families, not line coverage.** The oracle maps each test run to a
subset of the spec's observations (behavior flags). Producing and interpreting that coverage is the
next step (Studio runs the stored oracle pass) — not your concern. Your job ends at "the oracle runs
and captures traces."

## The `quint oracle` interface (complete reference)

### The config file

The whole run is described in `quint-oracle.<key>.json` (format `"quint-oracle-config"`, version
`1`) so you invoke `quint oracle --config quint-oracle.<key>.json` instead of ~15 flags. Quint Studio
watches this file. **The draft already exists** (written at generate, observations user-confirmed);
your task is to **add `testCommand` (and `buildCommand` if the tests need a rebuild first), and
confirm `reportDir`** — leaving `observations`/`observationGroups`, `spec`, `main`, and
`actionNameMap` untouched except to add missing event-to-action routes you discover while wiring.
**Relative paths resolve against the config file's directory**, and the `testCommand` is
spawned from that directory, so relative script paths keep working from any cwd.

The keys you add/own at this stage are `testCommand` and `buildCommand`; the rest of the table
below was already filled in at generate (read it, don't rewrite it):

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `format` | `"quint-oracle-config"` (required) |
| `version` | `1` (required) |
| `spec` | path to the `.qnt` (stands in for the input positional) |
| `main` | main module name (omit to auto-guess); needed when the spec is imported under a wrapper |
| `actionNameMap` | MBT replay routing, `{ loggedEvent: [QuintAction, ...] }`; omit entries when names already match; one logged event may map to multiple spec actions |
| `eventScope` | Studio-owned component key used to select explicitly-scoped log events before replay. Read it and use the exact value when constructing the component logger; never change it during wiring/refinement |
| `unguidedStepBudget` | max alternatives for one missing replay pick; Studio default is `10` |
| `stepReplayBudget` | max missing-pick alternatives across one logged step; Studio default is `50` |
| `observations` | flat list of observation `val` names — their first-firing order names the behavior classes |
| `observationGroups` | `{ key: { name, observations } }` for per-group projected coverage; groups may overlap. Members are folded into the effective observation list automatically, so a fully-grouped run needs no separate `observations` key |
| `components` | explicit `{ key: { name, observations } }` partition (auto-detected if omitted) |
| `testCommand` | the test command, **array form** (`["jest", "cart.spec.ts"]`); spawned from the config dir. Select whole files/targets, not an enumerated test-name list — this command defines the suite every future run rebuilds coverage from, and a pinned name list silently excludes tests added later (test generation appends to these files) |
| `buildCommand` | optional **array-form** command run from the config dir BEFORE the tests, so tests exercise freshly-built code (e.g. a compiled `dist`); a non-zero exit aborts the run. Scope it to rebuild every package exercised by this component's tests so the run uses the current instrumentation |
| `reportDir` | where `report.json` is written |
| `studio.broadTestCommand` | the promote-time broad run, **array form** like `testCommand` — every test across the targets exercising this spec (incl. any integration-test target). PARALLEL by default (buffered logs are test-tagged, so parallel workers/processes attribute correctly); force **serial** only for suites that live-log (see the parallelism note below). At **promote** Studio runs it **verbatim** for ANY test runner (it carries no per-runner knowledge). Scope it with the runner's own flags — e.g. Jest `["jest","cart/","sync/"]`, pytest `["pytest","tests/cart","tests/sync"]`, Rust `["cargo","nextest","run","-p","cart","-p","integration"]` (add `--runInBand` / `-p no:xdist` / `--test-threads=1` only for a live-logging suite). Omit → promote reuses `testCommand` as-is, so scope THAT broadly enough. **Must live UNDER `studio`** — quint's strict parser rejects unknown top-level keys; `studio` is passed through |
| `randomSteps`, `maxSteps`, `maxSamples`, `agrStrategy`, `agrConfig` | run-shape settings (CLI flags override these) |
| `studio` | `{ system, model }` metadata embedded in the report for Quint Studio |

Note: the keys are `observations` / `observationGroups`. The old names `tracks` / `trackGroups` are
rejected with an explicit error. Set `reportDir` to a **new** directory for this component (do not
reuse another component's).

```json
  "observationGroups": {
    "lifecycle": { "name": "Cart lifecycle", "observations": ["cart_completed", "item_removed_from_cart"] },
    "inventory": { "name": "Inventory protection", "observations": ["last_unit_added", "inventory_depleted"] }
  },
  "reportDir": "mc-out-cart",
  "studio": { "system": "Medusa Cart", "model": "quint-specs/cart.qnt" },
  "testCommand": ["node", "node_modules/.bin/jest", "__tests__/cart"]
}
```

### Invocation and precedence

The first run rides `confirm_wired`; re-runs go through `run_quint_oracle(pipeline_key)` —
either way Studio runs `quint oracle --config quint-oracle.<key>.json --max-samples 100` for you.

CLI flags win over config values, so keep the test command in the config — Studio's
run passes only the config, the report dir, and the pinned sample cap.

### What a run does

1. Runs `buildCommand` (if any) from the config dir; a non-zero exit aborts.
2. Starts the oracle **HTTP daemon** and exports `QUINT_ORACLE_URL` into the test process.
3. Spawns `testCommand` (from the config dir). Your instrumented code POSTs/PUTs traces to the daemon.
4. After the tests exit, the daemon validates each captured trace against the spec, then shuts down.
5. Writes `report.json` to `reportDir` (run metadata + observation docs are extracted from the spec
   automatically — Studio needs no separate spec access).

### The daemon HTTP protocol (what the oracle client talks to)

- `POST /test/<name>` — begin a test; `<name>` becomes the trace's test name in the report.
- `PUT  /log` — body `{ "action": "<logged name>", "arguments": [ { "name", "value", "domain?" } ], "scopes": ["<component-key>"] }`.
  An argument `{ "name": "outcome", "value": "rejected" }` marks the event a **rejected attempt**:
  it replays as a stutter (no transition) and counts as tested evidence for the matching guard
  scenario (see Phase 2).
- `POST /validate`, `POST /shutdown` — internal; the CLI handles these.

`QUINT_ORACLE_URL` is set by `quint oracle` in the test **child** process before it spawns. **The
oracle must spawn the test command — never the other way around.** If the app process is already
running (e.g. loaded by a test framework) before the env var exists, the client captures
`QUINT_ORACLE_URL` as `undefined` for the whole run and the oracle receives **zero** traces.

### The report

`report.json` in `reportDir` groups tests into **behavior families** (observation combinations that
fired together). Open it with `quint report <reportDir>`. Each test entry has `matched: true|false`;
failures carry a text you classify (see the validation loop). Studio re-imports this report.

## Phase 1: Write / extend the Oracle Client

The client reads `QUINT_ORACLE_URL` (no-op when unset), exposes `startTest(name)` (POSTs `/test/<name>`)
and `scope(componentKey)`, whose logger sends `logAction(action, args)` to `/log` with that component
scope. Each arg is `{ name, value, domain? }`:
- `name` matches the parameter name in the Quint action signature (copy from the spec)
- `value` is the concrete value
- `domain` is the Quint constant set the value belongs to (e.g. `"USERS"`, `"ITEMS"`)

If the repo already has an oracle client (another component set one up), reuse it — only extend its
action/domain mapping to cover this component's actions. Otherwise:

- **Rust, TypeScript or Go** — call the **`vendor_oracle_client` MCP tool** with the language. Studio
  writes the client library into `quint-specs/oracle-client/<language>/` (Rust: a local crate;
  TypeScript: a local no-build npm package; Go: a local module wired with a replace directive) and
  its response tells you exactly how to consume it
  (path/file/replace dependency + import + call-site snippets). Never copy-paste an HTTP client, never
  path-depend into a Quint checkout, and never edit files under `quint-specs/oracle-client/` —
  they are Studio-managed and get committed with the repo so instrumentation works on other
  machines. Guard rule for Rust: bind `let _t = start_test(…)` and HOLD it for the whole test
  scope; buffered (sync) tests may run fully parallel — only async/actor tests whose transitions
  live-log off the test thread need `--test-threads=1`. For TypeScript: `const t =
  startTest(name)` in the shared beforeEach, `await t.end()` in afterEach; parallel jest/vitest
  workers are fine (tagged flushes), but avoid `test.concurrent` within one file and add
  `--runInBand` only when logging is live. For Go: `g := StartTest(t.Name())` with
  `t.Cleanup(g.End)` in each test; avoid `t.Parallel()` within a package, while `go test ./...`
  package-parallelism is fine.
- **Any other language / a crate that can't take the dep** — Read
  [`guidelines/oracle-client.md`](guidelines/oracle-client.md): it specifies the protocol and the
  attribution semantics a custom client MUST replicate.

## Phase 2: Instrument the application code (+ a test boundary)

**Delegate site DISCOVERY to the `quint-instrumentation-scout` subagent (Agent tool) first**: pass it
the action list (names + args + domains from the spec / draft config) and the app source
root; it returns a per-action `file:line` site table, the shared test-boundary hook point, and any
unplaceable actions — without filling your context with the codebase sweep. You then make the edits
at the sites it found (spot-check a site if it looks off; the scout is read-only).

**The `logAction` instrumentation goes in the application code — never in test code, and never as a
new test.** Find the single point in the application where each state transition completes and insert
the `logAction` call there (you identified these call sites while modelling; the scout re-locates
them if needed). **Log completed transitions only — and tag rejected attempts.** An untagged
`logAction` asserts "this transition HAPPENED", so it fires only after the state change completes.
When the code REJECTS an operation the spec guards (an early return, a thrown validation error —
the reject side of a guard conjunct), do NOT emit a normal transition event on the reject path:
emit the **same action name and args tagged with an `outcome` argument whose value is
`"rejected"`** (`{ name: "outcome", value: "rejected" }`). A rejected-tagged event replays as a
**stutter** — no transition — and marks the matching guard scenario as tested: the tests exercised
the contract and the code held. Never invent a second `<op>_rejected` event name or
`actionNameMap` entry — one operation, one action name; the `outcome` tag is the only
discriminator. An **untagged** logged transition whose inputs falsify the action's guard replays
as a **violation finding** — the code performed a transition its contract forbids; that is the
finding this pipeline exists to make, never something to fix by loosening or widening the guard.
Keep logging success-only for *internal/unmodeled* failures (a bubbled-up plumbing error the spec
doesn't model is a disabled action — nothing to log).
Construct a scoped logger from the config's exact `eventScope` and use that logger for every event
owned by this component. If one successful transition genuinely belongs to multiple component
abstractions, target all of their keys explicitly. Do not add unrelated actions to `actionNameMap`
and do not leave calls unscoped to make a report pass. The oracle rejects unscoped events; every
instrumentation event must declare its owner.
The existing tests then feed traces automatically just by exercising that code. Choose a
`testCommand` that runs existing tests covering this component's behavior; do not create test files,
cases, or fixtures.

**Do not add oracle calls to test helper functions.** The only test-side change is the per-test
`startTest` boundary below, wired through one shared hook.

### Where to instrument

| Application style | Instrumentation point |
|---|---|
| Express / HTTP server | Response middleware that fires after a successful route handler |
| Service / store layer | Inside the service method, after the state mutation, before returning |
| Event-driven / CQRS | Event store `emit()`/`commit()` after the command is accepted |
| Actor model | Inside `handle()` after applying the state update |
| CLI tool | After each command function returns without error |

### Test boundaries are essential — without them, the oracle captures nothing

The oracle needs one `startTest(name)` per test so it records one trace per test. Wire this through a
**single shared hook** — e.g. a `beforeEach` in the suite's existing setup file, or the project's
existing `oracleStartTest`-style helper — rather than editing tests one by one (`Grep` for
`QUINT_ORACLE_URL` to find how this repo already does it, and reuse it). This is the only test-side
touch, and it adds no new tests. Without per-test boundaries the oracle records **zero** traces.

### Express middleware pattern (TypeScript)

```typescript
// src/middleware/oracle-middleware.ts
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { scope, OracleArg } from 'quint-oracle-client';

const oracle = scope('cart'); // exact eventScope from quint-oracle.cart.json

export interface OracleTrace { action: string; args: OracleArg[]; }

export function oracleMiddleware(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
  const originalJson = res.json.bind(res);
  res.json = function (body: unknown) {
    const trace: OracleTrace | undefined = res.locals.oracleTrace;
    if (trace && res.statusCode === 200) {
      oracle.logAction(trace.action, trace.args).catch(() => {}); // fire-and-forget
    }
    return originalJson(body);
  };
  next();
}
```

```typescript
// in each route handler, before res.json():
res.locals.oracleTrace = {
  action: 'add_to_cart',
  args: [
    { name: 'user', value: user, domain: 'USERS' },
    { name: 'item', value: itemName, domain: 'ITEMS' },
  ],
};
```

### Service layer pattern (Rust / Go / any language)

```rust
impl ShopService {
    pub fn add_to_cart(&mut self, user: &str, item: &str) -> Result<Cart, ShopError> {
        let args = [
            OracleArg { name: "user", value: user.into(), domain: Some("USERS") },
            OracleArg { name: "item", value: item.into(), domain: Some("ITEMS") },
        ];
        match self.state.add_item(user, item) {
            Ok(updated) => {
                oracle_client::scope(&["cart"]).log_action("add_to_cart", &args); // completed transition
                Ok(updated)
            }
            // The spec GUARDS this operation → tag the rejected attempt (it replays as a
            // stutter and marks the guard scenario tested). Never log a reject as a plain
            // transition — the transition didn't happen. (A rejection of an operation the
            // spec doesn't model: don't log at all.)
            Err(e) => {
                let mut rejected = args.to_vec();
                rejected.push(OracleArg { name: "outcome", value: "rejected".into(), domain: None });
                oracle_client::scope(&["cart"]).log_action("add_to_cart", &rejected);
                Err(e)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### State-conformance facts — make model-code fidelity ENFORCEABLE

Trace replay checks that each logged action is *admissible* in the model (name + pinned args
satisfy the guards); it never compares post-state. So a model whose update logic quietly diverges
from the code — the classic slip is modeling an operation's *intent* instead of its actual writes
— replays green forever. Close that hole per mutating operation:

1. **In the code**: after the mutation, log ONE abstracted post-state fact as an extra argument —
   something cheap, deterministic, and computable in the model's abstraction. Collection **size**
   is the workhorse (`leaf_count: self.num_leaves()`); emptiness flags and abstract enums also
   work. Never a hash or anything below the model's abstraction level.
2. **In the spec**: the action takes the fact as a parameter **named exactly as the logged
   argument** and **guards on equality with the model-computed post-state**; `step` supplies it via
   a singleton nondet so simulation pays nothing:

   ```quint
   // step:
   nondet observed_count = Set(count_after_insert(leaves, key, value)).oneOf()
   ...
   insert(key, value, observed_count)

   // action — parameter name matches the logged arg (`leaf_count`); the pick it
   // is passed (`observed_count`) can be called anything:
   action insert(key: int, value: int, leaf_count: int): bool = all {
     leaf_count == count_after_insert(leaves, key, value),  // conformance guard
     ...
   }
   ```

   In simulation the singleton makes the guard free. At replay the pick is **pinned to the
   code's logged fact** — if the model's update disagrees with the code's, the guard fails, the
   trace lands UNMATCHED, and the pipeline routes to refine instead of quietly reaching ready.
   The pin is what makes this a test at all: a fact the logged name cannot reach leaves the pick
   free, the singleton satisfies itself, and the trace matches while checking nothing. The oracle
   log says so — `guidance for "<test>": N/M logged args pin a step nondet`, plus an explicit
   warning naming the args that reach no pick.
   That unmatched trace is the fidelity test: investigate whether the MODEL is unfaithful (fix
   the model to mirror the code and let a correctness property state the intent) before touching
   anything else.

Give every state-MUTATING instrumented operation at least one conformance fact. Read-only
operations need none.

### Instrumentation checklist

- [ ] `logAction` fires on completed transitions only; **rejections of guarded operations carry the
      `outcome: "rejected"` tag** (same action name); nothing logged for internal/unmodeled failures
- [ ] every state-MUTATING operation logs at least one **state-conformance fact** (see above) that the spec guards on
- [ ] every logged argument name matches the spec action's parameter name (or the pick's own name), so it PINS — check the run's `N/M logged args pin a step nondet` line; an unpinned conformance fact checks nothing
- [ ] every new/refined call uses a scoped logger whose key exactly matches config `eventScope`
- [ ] multi-component scopes are used only when the transition genuinely belongs to each component
- [ ] action names match the spec's logged-action names exactly (copy from the spec)
- [ ] argument `name` fields match the Quint parameter names exactly
- [ ] `domain` fields match the Quint constant-set names exactly
- [ ] `startTest(name)` is called once per test
