71	# quint-specs/notes-store.qnt's KEYS/VALUES_ALL are kept small (a wider domain OOM-crashed
72	# the evaluator — see the spec's own doc comment), so every categorizer below maps onto a
73	# SINGLE representative slot per shape rather than one slot per distinct real value. That
74	# gives up per-test distinctness beyond what's noted per-function; a specific replay
75	# mismatch from a test that legitimately needs more is a refine-loop fix, not a reason to
76	# widen these lists again.
77	_NOTES_OWNABLE_KEY_SLOTS = ["d-bounty", "d-busy"]
78	_NOTES_DID_SLOTS = ["did:key:alice", "did:key:bob", "did:key:mallory"]

82	    return ns if ns in _NOTES_RESERVED_NS else store.TOPIC_NS

87	    ownable ("d-*", not in UNOWNABLE_ROOMS) real room gets a per-test slot from
88	    OWNABLE_KEYS (so two different owners/claims in one test still land on distinct model
89	    rooms), and a non-ownable real room always maps to "lobby" — matching store.ownable()'s
90	    own real verdict rather than guessing from the name. Every other (generic,
91	    world-writable) namespace collapses onto the model's single "topic" namespace

93	    writing more than one distinct generic note has its second/third write alias the
94	    first's identity, which is the collision this domain size accepts."""
95	    if ns in _NOTES_RESERVED_NS:

108	    that CAS-compares (`if=<value>`) two DIFFERENT real plain values in the same test loses
109	    that distinction at this domain size (see the spec's doc comment)."""
110	    tokens = value.split()

112	        if len(tokens) == 1:
113	            return oracle_client.categorize("notes-store-did", value, _NOTES_DID_SLOTS)
114	        return "list_ok"
115	    if any(didkey.is_did(t) for t in tokens):
116	        return "list_bad"
117	    return "plain"

123	    claims, and an attacker signing with a different real key gets a different slot — the
124	    relational fact gateOk's `signerOpt == Some(value)` / `== Some(unwrap(current))`
125	    conjuncts actually check."""
126	    return oracle_client.categorize("notes-store-did", signer, _NOTES_DID_SLOTS)
127

"""agent-chat: an HTTP-native, zero-auth chat + notes server for restricted agents.

Every operation — including writes — is reachable with a single plain GET, because
that is the only verb most LLM harnesses expose (`webfetch`). Responses are
text/plain by default so markdown/HTML converters in those harnesses cannot mangle
them; `?format=json` is available for programmatic callers.

Not part of the FLOP protocol. Satellite service, ephemeral by design.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import secrets
import time
import tomllib
from collections import OrderedDict
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.concurrency import run_in_threadpool
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse, Response
from starlette.routing import Route

import didkey
import manifest
import oracle_client
import store
from store import StoreConflictError, StoreError

ROOT = Path(os.environ.get("CHAT_ROOT", "/data"))

# "rooms" matches quint-oracle.rooms.json's eventScope exactly — the oracle rejects
# unscoped events, and any other value would silently exclude every log below from replay.
_rooms_oracle = oracle_client.scope("rooms")
# "notes-store" matches quint-oracle.notes-store.json's eventScope exactly.
_notes_oracle = oracle_client.scope("notes-store")
# "did-key-identity" matches quint-oracle.did-key-identity.json's eventScope exactly.
# didkey.py logs its own four actions (public_key/is_did/abbreviate/verify) under this
# same scope key; only `_signer` — app.py's, not didkey.py's — is instrumented here.
_signer_oracle = oracle_client.scope("did-key-identity")


def _text_oracle_category(stored_text: str) -> str:
    """The message-length bucket quint-specs/rooms.qnt's `textLen` abstracts every
    message into ("empty" / "short" / "at-limit" / "over-limit") — the model tracks ring
    bytes by this bucket, not by literal content, so real message text (arbitrarily
    varied across tests, unlike the model's tiny domain) is never logged verbatim; this
    is what the `text` argument actually carries to the oracle."""
    n = len(stored_text)
    if n == 0:
        return "empty"
    if n < store.MAX_TEXT_CHARS:
        return "short"
    return "at-limit" if n == store.MAX_TEXT_CHARS else "over-limit"


# quint-specs/notes-store.qnt's NS_SET pins the three reserved namespaces literally and
# collapses every other (world-writable) namespace into "topic" — gateOk's generic branch
# treats them identically, and topic is itself one of the real reserved-but-plain
# namespaces the wired tests already use.
_NOTES_RESERVED_NS = (store.OWNERS_NS, store.ALLOW_NS, store.NONCE_NS)
# quint-specs/notes-store.qnt's KEYS/VALUES_ALL are kept small (a wider domain OOM-crashed
# the evaluator — see the spec's own doc comment), so every categorizer below maps onto a
# SINGLE representative slot per shape rather than one slot per distinct real value. That
# gives up per-test distinctness beyond what's noted per-function; a specific replay
# mismatch from a test that legitimately needs more is a refine-loop fix, not a reason to
# widen these lists again.
_NOTES_OWNABLE_KEY_SLOTS = ["d-bounty", "d-busy"]
_NOTES_DID_SLOTS = ["did:key:alice", "did:key:bob", "did:key:mallory"]


def _note_ns_oracle_category(ns: str) -> str:
    return ns if ns in _NOTES_RESERVED_NS else store.TOPIC_NS


def _note_key_oracle_category(ns: str, key: str) -> str:
    """Room ids under a reserved namespace are load-bearing identity (ownership/CAS): an
    ownable ("d-*", not in UNOWNABLE_ROOMS) real room gets a per-test slot from
    OWNABLE_KEYS (so two different owners/claims in one test still land on distinct model
    rooms), and a non-ownable real room always maps to "lobby" — matching store.ownable()'s
    own real verdict rather than guessing from the name. Every other (generic,
    world-writable) namespace collapses onto the model's single "topic" namespace
    (_note_ns_oracle_category) and its key onto the one "note1" representative — a test
    writing more than one distinct generic note has its second/third write alias the
    first's identity, which is the collision this domain size accepts."""
    if ns in _NOTES_RESERVED_NS:
        if store.ownable(key):
            return oracle_client.categorize("notes-store-ownable-key", key, _NOTES_OWNABLE_KEY_SLOTS)
        return "lobby"
    return "note1"


def _note_value_oracle_category(value: str) -> str:
    """quint-specs/notes-store.qnt's VALUES_ALL: a single did:key-shaped value gets a
    per-test DIDS slot (so self-claims/hand-overs and forgeries both survive
    categorization — the same real did:key within one test always maps to the same slot),
    a space-separated list of did:keys becomes "list_ok", one with any non-did token
    becomes "list_bad", and everything else becomes the single "plain" bucket — a test
    that CAS-compares (`if=<value>`) two DIFFERENT real plain values in the same test loses
    that distinction at this domain size (see the spec's doc comment)."""
    tokens = value.split()
    if tokens and all(didkey.is_did(t) for t in tokens):
        if len(tokens) == 1:
            return oracle_client.categorize("notes-store-did", value, _NOTES_DID_SLOTS)
        return "list_ok"
    if any(didkey.is_did(t) for t in tokens):
        return "list_bad"
    return "plain"


def _note_signer_oracle_category(signer: str) -> str:
    """The signer DID uses the SAME per-test slot cache as `value` (kind "notes-store-did"):
    a signer proving its own key for a first claim logs the identical slot as the value it
    claims, and an attacker signing with a different real key gets a different slot — the
    relational fact gateOk's `signerOpt == Some(value)` / `== Some(unwrap(current))`
    conjuncts actually check."""
    return oracle_client.categorize("notes-store-did", signer, _NOTES_DID_SLOTS)


def _note_nonce_oracle_token(nonce: str | int) -> str:
    """quint-specs/notes-store.qnt's NONCE_TOKENS = n0..n3, ordered by nonceValue(); the
    wired tests only ever use small sequential nonces, so clamping to the top token for
    anything beyond is lossy only in a case no wired test exercises."""
    try:
        n = int(nonce)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return "n0"
    return f"n{max(0, min(n, 3))}"

def refund(request: Request, kind: str, per_min: float, burst: float | None = None) -> None:
    """Hand one token back to the caller's bucket, capped at its burst.

    `last` is deliberately left alone: it is the refill clock, and moving it would either
    grant free time or discard earned time. Only the balance changes.
    """
    ip = client_ip(request)
    cap = float(per_min if burst is None else burst)
    tokens, last = _buckets.get((ip, kind), (cap, time.monotonic()))
    _buckets[(ip, kind)] = (min(cap, tokens + 1.0), last)

class HeaderLimits:
    """Reject oversized header blocks at the app edge, precisely.

    The parser cap (`--h11-max-incomplete-event-size`) is real but fuzzy: it bounds
    *buffered incomplete* data, so a block that arrives in one segment slips under it —
    measured, httptools returned 200 for a 256 KiB header. This is the deterministic
    bound, and it also documents the contract. It does not replace the parser cap, which
    is what stops the bytes being buffered in the first place.
    """

    def __init__(self, app):
        self.app = app

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
        if scope["type"] == "http":
            headers = scope.get("headers", [])
            total = sum(len(k) + len(v) + 4 for k, v in headers)
            if len(headers) > MAX_HEADERS or total > MAX_HEADER_BYTES:
                body = (
                    f"431 header block too large: {len(headers)} headers / {total} bytes "
                    f"(max {MAX_HEADERS} / {MAX_HEADER_BYTES}). This service needs none of "
                    f"them — a plain GET with no custom headers is the whole protocol.\n"
                )
                await Response(
                    body,
                    status_code=431,
                    media_type="text/plain; charset=utf-8",
                    headers={"Cache-Control": "no-store"},
                )(scope, receive, send)
                return
        await self.app(scope, receive, send)

findings.reasoning: Grepped tests/test_app.py for every waiter-related test (wait=, _waiter_slot, asyncio.gather, ThreadPoolExecutor) — the only one is test_waiter_slots_are_bounded_per_ip (app.py:1654-1666 in the current tree), which nests app._waiter_slot() calls directly: a,b,c,d on '1.2.3.4' (4 concurrent, matches MAX_WAITERS_PER_IP=4 exactly) then 'other' on '5.6.7.8' (5th concurrent, different IP), before any release fires. Peak concurrency in this trace is 5. MAX_WAITERS_TOTAL in the model is 8 (deliberately not the real 64 — see the spec's own comment on that const — to keep the identity domain small enough for MAX_BUCKETS eviction testing elsewhere in the same spec), so reaching it would need at least 8 concurrently-held slots with zero releases interleaved, which no existing test drives at any scale (real or modeled). This is not a setup/instrumentation problem: the guard `_waiters_total >= MAX_WAITERS_TOTAL` (app.py:1012) is real and reachable in principle — the real code just has no test anywhere near that concurrency.
findings.summary: No test drives enough concurrent long-polls to hit the global waiter cap (8 in the model, 64 in production) — the per-IP cap is tested, the global one isn't. Coverage gap only; the code path is real and harmless when it fires.

findings.reasoning: The real _waiter_slot (app.py:1004-1025) is a @contextmanager: the `finally:` block that decrements _waiters_total/_waiters_by_ip is lexically INSIDE the same function invocation as the `try: yield True` that only runs after _waiters_total/_waiters_by_ip were just incremented for that exact call. Python's context-manager protocol guarantees __exit__ (and therefore this finally) only ever runs paired with a completed __enter__ of the SAME instance — there is no caller-reachable way to invoke the release half without its own matching acquire immediately before it in the same call stack. The spec models acquire (_waiter_slot) and release (_waiter_release) as two independent, freely-interleavable actions (a deliberate modeling choice — see the spec's doc comment on _waiter_release — so the model can represent overlapping concurrent holds across different callers), which is MORE permissive than the real code: it admits a release-with-no-prior-acquire-for-this-ip state the real code cannot reach through any public entry point. Confirmed this isn't a setup issue: instrumentation logs _waiter_release only from inside the real finally block (so it can never fire without a preceding logged _waiter_slot grant for that ip), and the guard itself (`waitersByIp.has(ip)`) is exactly the real code's implicit pairing invariant.
findings.summary: The 'release without a matching acquire' case the model can express has no real code path that can trigger it — Python's context-manager scoping pairs every release with its own acquire. Not testable, and not a risk.

findings.reasoning: reject_oversized_headers only has one call site: inside HeaderLimits.__call__ (app.py:835-852 in the current tree), on the branch where `len(headers) > MAX_HEADERS or total > MAX_HEADER_BYTES` is already true — the else path just calls `await self.app(scope, receive, send)` and returns, touching no oracle log call at all. There is no code site where an 'attempted reject_oversized_headers but the guard was false' event could be logged, because an undersized header block is not an attempt at THIS action in any sense the app's control flow expresses — it's simply a normal request that never reaches this branch. This mirrors guardId 682's finding: the guard's false side is real (it's the normal-request path, exercised by all 156 tests constantly) but it has no distinct transition of ITS OWN to log against this action.
findings.summary: Every ordinary request exercises the 'headers are fine' path, but there's no code site that logs it as an attempt on this specific reject action — a normal request just isn't an attempt to reject headers. Structural, not a real gap.

findings.reasoning: Same underlying guard and same action (reject_oversized_headers) as guardId 733/ruleId ...|256 above — this is the simulator's other rule-instance of the identical headerLimitsReject(headerCount, totalBytes) conjunct (app.py:839's single `or` condition, modeled as one pure def). Same reasoning applies verbatim: the only call site is the rejecting branch itself; the passing branch (app.py:852) never touches this action's log call, so there is no way to log a guard-false attempt at this action specifically.
findings.summary: Duplicate of the other reject_oversized_headers guard-scenario finding — same single guard, same reason: a passing header check isn't a loggable attempt at the reject action.
